Q: Ninja Build System + gcc/clang doesn't output diagnostic colors A:

Another cause is that if Ninja itself doesn't see a terminal, such as when you pipe it into Less, it removes color codes from its buffered subprocess output. The way Ninja supports disabling this is with an environment variable:

env CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 ninja | less -r

This also happens if you have Ninja running under Ninja. Which is normally a thing not to do, except: As a quirk of CMake, it is impossible to make the test target depend on unittests being up to date (like you would expect if you come from Meson), so the workaround is to invoke Ninja from a Ctest hook. Which is run by ninja test. Boom, you are running Ninja under Ninja, so that hook actually needs a cmake -E env CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 prefix.

To summarize:

  • Gcc needs -fdiagnostics-color=always
  • Clang needs -fcolor-diagnostics
    • Windows needs -fansi-escape-codes
  • Ninja needs env CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 ninja …

Q: How to set absolute session timeout for a Spring Session A:

This feature is not implemented in Spring sessions.

A request for this feature at https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-session/issues/922 was rejected, with this workaround provided:

You could provide a delegating implementation of the SessionRepository interface that delegates to another implementation of SessionRepository (i.e. Redis) and then when it retrieves the session determines if the creation date is past the absolute session timeout. If it is, then you would invalidate the session and return a null value for the lookup.

(More implementation details are discussed in the issue comments.)

Q: How do I get started coding HTML Applications (HTA) for game development A:

HTAs are old technology, but they still work in Windows 11. They provide a way for mere mortals to create local GUI apps that have access to all of the machine's resources (i.e. file system and registry). However, with AI help, it is now relatively easy, for anyone with some programming ability, to use Visual Studio Community to create GUI apps in C# instead and that, IMO, is a better way to go (which is what I've transitioned to).

If you still want to try your hand at HTAs, it's important to understand what they are and what limitations you're up against.

HTAs run via MSHTA.exe which uses MSHTML and JScript and/or VBScript. MSHTML is the same engine that's used by Internet Explorer, so you are limited to the capabilities of IE 11.

Also note that you can create HTML applications using VBSEdit. Don't let the "VBS" part throw you. VBSEdit is an IDE that lets your create and debug HTML applications that are nearly identical to HTAs but with enhancements (e.g. built in file open/save dialog support). You can save the project as an Exe which allows it to run without any dependency on MSHTA.exe (which is blocked by some organizations). WinSetView is an example of a VBSEdit HTML application.

You can find many HTA examples online, including my GitHub page. I have some big programs that use the technology, but you should probably start by looking at some of the examples here.

Technical stuff to get started:

A basic HTA, that just starts with an <html> tag will actually run in IE 5 mode. If you add a <!DOCTYPE html> header, it will run in IE 7 mode. And adding <http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=9"> will run it in IE 9 mode, which is the highest mode supported by the optional hta:application section. If you don't need the settings offered by that section, you can change content="IE=9" to content="IE=11" to run in IE 11 mode. Be sure to use JScript and not VBScript, as the latter only goes up to IE=10 mode and is scheduled to no longer be installed in Windows, by default, starting sometime in 2027.

Note that if you use VBSEdit, it will set up the skeleton code for you and ensure you're running with IE 11 capabilities (use extension "HTM" instead of extension "HTA").
